stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
stages.hook: Why can a single Turkish verb form mean both 'he came' and 'apparently he came'?
explain: Turkish grammar marks the source of information. The past -di is used for events the speaker witnessed: 'Geldi' (He came, I saw it). The past -miş is used for events learned by hearsay, inference or surprise: 'Gelmiş' (He has come, apparently). This is called evidentiality. Compare 'Yağmur yağdı' (I saw it rain) and 'Yağmur yağmış' (It seems it rained: I see wet streets).

Beyond tense, verbs carry voice (passive -ıl, causative -dır, reflexive -ın, reciprocal -ış), negation (-ma), ability (-ebil), and mood (-sa conditional, -meli necessitative). Turkish is usually described as having six core cases (nominative, accusative, dative, locative, ablative, genitive); the instrumental -le is sometimes counted as well. Stem, voice, negation, ability, tense, person form a fixed order: yaz-dır-ıl-ma-dı (it was not made to be written).
stages.mnemonic: -di: I saw. -miş: they say, or I infer.
items: It was not made to be written
sentences: It seems it rained last night.

o: The speaker did not witness it
The speaker saw it happen directly
It is a future tense form
It is an order to the listener
gq.why: The suffix -miş marks information the speaker did not see directly.

gq.q: How many core cases is Turkish usually said to have?
gq.why: Grammars usually list six: nominative, accusative, dative, locative, ablative and genitive (the instrumental -le is sometimes added).

panel.q: Why is 'Yağmur yağmış' natural when you see wet roads?
o: You saw the rain falling yourself
You infer the rain from evidence
panel.why: The wet roads are evidence, so the speaker uses -miş to say it must have rained.

o: Makes the verb passive and impersonal
panel.why: -dır makes someone cause the action, as in yazdırmak, to have something written.

panel.q: Which order is correct for voice and negation?
panel.why: Voice precedes negation, then tense.

teach.model: The past -di marks witnessed events; -miş marks hearsay or inference. Verb suffixes follow a fixed order: voice, negation, ability, tense, person.

stages.title: Historical development of the language
stages.hook: Why do Turkish texts from the Ottoman era look so different from modern Turkish?
explain: Turkish belongs to the Turkic family. The oldest large texts are the Orkhon inscriptions (8th century CE) in a runic script. Old Anatolian Turkish developed from the 13th to the 15th centuries, and Ottoman Turkish (until the early 20th century) was written in Arabic script and contained many Arabic and Persian words and grammar.

In 1928 the Latin alphabet replaced the Arabic script, and in 1932 the Turkish Language Association (TDK) began to promote native words and standardisation. The result: modern Turkish is easier to read and phonetically written, though older texts need transcription. Ottoman had high register (divan literature) and low register (folk speech).
stages.mnemonic: Orkhon stone, Ottoman script, Latin letters, TDK.
sentences: The language has a long history.

gq.q: When was the Latin alphabet introduced?
Which inscriptions are the oldest major Turkic texts?

o: They are shorter than the old letters

panel.why: A phonetic script is easier.

o: They are written in English letters

teach.model: Old Turkic (Orkhon inscriptions), Old Anatolian, Ottoman Turkish, then the 1928 Latin alphabet and the 1932 TDK.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
stages.hook: How do Turkish poems from the court differ from those of village minstrels?
explain: Turkish literature has two long traditions: divan poetry (court poetry using Persian-Arabic forms and metres, by poets like Fuzuli and Baki) and folk poetry (halk edebiyatı, by minstrels called âşık, such as Karacaoğlan, using syllabic metre and simple language; Yunus Emre also wrote simple syllabic verse, in the related mystic tradition). Aşık Veysel is a 20th-century folk poet who sang with a saz.

Modernisation began with the Tanzimat reforms (1839): authors such as Şinasi and Namık Kemal wrote plays, newspapers and novels. In the Republic, Nazım Hikmet, Orhan Veli, Yaşar Kemal and Orhan Pamuk shaped modern literature. Cultural discourse today includes debates about language purity, identity and translation.
stages.mnemonic: Divan for the court, âşık for the village, novel for the modern city.
sentences: The novel appeared in the nineteenth century.

gq.why: Yunus Emre wrote simple, syllabic verse in the folk and mystic tradition, unlike Fuzuli and Baki (court poets) or Şinasi (a Tanzimat reformer).

gq.q: What marks the Tanzimat in literature?
o: Only oral poetry from the villages
No change at all in forms

panel.q: Why do divan and folk poetry differ?
o: They are really the same tradition
panel.why: Divan poetry served the educated court; folk poetry belonged to ordinary people and minstrels.
The saz is a long-necked lute.

panel.q: Why do debates on 'language purity' matter?
o: They end the use of the language
They are about spelling reform only
They are about speed of speech
panel.why: What a community thinks of its words reflects how it sees itself.

teach.model: Divan poetry served the court. Folk poetry belongs to minstrels (âşık). The Tanzimat brought novels, plays and newspapers.

trip.prompt: Read about divan and folk poetry.

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
stages.hook: How do you write the abstract of a Turkish research article?
explain: An abstract (özet) states the aim, method, findings and conclusion in 150–250 words. Standard phrases: 'Bu çalışmanın amacı ... incelemektir' (The aim of this study is to examine ...), 'Araştırmada ... yöntemi kullanılmıştır' (In the research ... method was used), 'Bulgular ... göstermiştir' (The findings showed ...).

Style: impersonal passive, nominalised verbs (-ma, -dığı), precise terms, and hedges. Citations follow a chosen style, e.g. (Yılmaz, 2020: 15). Keep the logic: purpose → method → results → implications. Avoid colloquial words and too many short sentences.
sentences: The aim of this study is to examine reading.
The findings showed a clear result.

gq.why: This formula states the aim of a study in the impersonal academic register.

panel.why: The passive keeps the focus on the research, not on the researcher.
Readers expect aim, method, results and implications in that logical order.

o: They are rare and hard to find
They are too long for abstracts
They are rude to the reader
panel.why: Colloquial words clash with the formal register expected in academic writing.

teach.model: State aim, method, findings, implications in passive impersonal style. Use Bu çalışmanın amacı ... incelemektir.

stages.title: Professional translation
stages.hook: How do you translate a legal or technical document into Turkish?
explain: Professional translation means accuracy, consistency and fitness for purpose. Use glossaries and translation memories, check terms in specialised sources and keep the register. Legal Turkish is formal, with long sentences, 'işbu' (this), 'aşağıda imzası bulunan' (the undersigned), 'taraflar' (the parties). Technical Turkish uses coined terms: 'yazılım', 'veri tabanı' (database), 'ağ' (network).

Quality control includes proofreading, comparing with the source, and checking numbers, dates and names. Beware false friends and calques. Turkish agglutination can make terms very long, so decide how to render English noun strings. Confidentiality and ethical codes are part of professional practice.

gq.why: A translation memory stores earlier source and target segments for reuse.

gq.q: What does 'taraflar' mean in a contract?

o: They are short and easy to see
They matter only in legal texts
panel.why: A wrong figure, date or name can change the legal or practical meaning of a document.

o: To add jokes to the text
panel.why: A glossary makes sure the same term is always translated the same way.

o: A grammar rule for borrowed words

panel.why: A calque copies the structure of a foreign phrase word for word, which often sounds unnatural.

teach.model: Use glossaries and translation memory, keep register, check numbers and terms, and respect confidentiality.

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
stages.hook: How can a polite sentence in Turkish hide a refusal?
explain: Complex communication often relies on implicature and politeness. 'Düşünürüz' (We will think about it) can mean a polite no. 'Bakarız' (We'll see) can be vague. Interpreters must catch tone, indirectness and honorifics, as well as content, and decide whether to make implied meaning explicit.

Turkish uses softeners: 'Acaba' (I wonder if), 'Belki', 'Rica etsem' (If I may ask), and the ability form for requests: 'Yardım edebilir misiniz?' (Could you help?) Use of siz, titles and ending -dir signals distance. In interpreting, preserve face-saving: translate politeness strategies, not just words.
stages.mnemonic: Say what they mean, not only what they say.
sentences: We will think about it, thank you.
If I may ask, where is the office?

gq.why: Düşünürüz literally means we will think, but it can be a polite way of declining.

o: A grammar case used in Turkish
A script used for old texts
A dialect of the Black Sea
gq.why: Implicature is what a speaker means beyond the words actually said.

panel.why: Tone and indirectness change what a sentence really communicates.

o: Hiding your face from the speaker
panel.why: Face-saving means protecting the dignity of the people in the conversation.

o: Yardım et bana, çabuk ol lütfen
panel.why: The softener rica etsem and the question form make the request less direct.

teach.model: Listen for implicature, tone and honorifics. Düşünürüz may mean no. Preserve politeness strategies.

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
stages.hook: Why do Anatolian, Balkan and Cypriot speakers sometimes sound so different?
explain: Dialectology studies variation. Turkish dialects can be grouped as Western (Rumeli, Aegean), Eastern Anatolian, Black Sea and others. Differences include sound shifts, vocabulary and intonation. Turkish belongs to the Oghuz branch of Turkic with Azerbaijani, Turkmen and Gagauz (spoken in Moldova).

Sociolinguistic variation includes age, class, urban or rural settings and style. Standard Turkish is based on Istanbul speech and used in education and media. Language contact has produced loans from Greek, Arabic, Persian, French and English. Diaspora communities in Germany show code-switching between Turkish and German.
stages.mnemonic: Standard in the centre, dialects around it.
sentences: Dialects differ in sound and vocabulary.
Standard Turkish is taught in school.

gq.q: Which language is in the Oghuz branch with Turkish?
gq.why: Azerbaijani, like Turkish, Turkmen and Gagauz, is an Oghuz Turkic language.

panel.why: A standard gives schools, media and administration a shared form of the language.

o: Writing secret codes in a text
Changing from one alphabet to another
panel.why: Code-switching means moving between two languages within a conversation, as in diaspora communities.

o: Only the region where people live
Only the age of the speaker
panel.why: Variation depends on region, age, class, setting and style together.

teach.model: Dialects vary by region and social factors. Standard Turkish rests on Istanbul speech. Turkish is in the Oghuz branch.

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
stages.hook: How do you say 'artificial intelligence' and 'database' in scientific Turkish?
explain: Scientific and technical Turkish combines coined native words and international terms. Examples: 'yapay zekâ' (artificial intelligence), 'veri tabanı' (database), 'yazılım' (software), 'donanım' (hardware), 'hücre' (cell), 'enerji' (energy), 'denklem' (equation). Terms are often compounds or derived with suffixes: 'bilişim' (informatics).

Style: precise, impersonal, with passive and nominal phrases: 'Deney yapılmıştır', 'Sonuçlar karşılaştırılmıştır'. Units follow the SI system. The Turkish Language Association publishes term dictionaries. Always check for established terms before coining your own.
stages.mnemonic: Check the term list before you coin a word.
sentences: The experiment was carried out in the laboratory.
The results were compared in the table.

gq.why: Veri tabanı is the established Turkish term for a database.
Bilişim is the Turkish word for informatics or information technology.

panel.q: Why is the passive common in science?
o: It is shorter than the active
It is more poetic in style
It is an older form of Turkish
panel.why: The passive focuses on what was done, which suits scientific writing.

panel.q: What should you do before coining a term?
panel.why: Established term lists keep scientific language consistent across texts.
Scientific writing in Turkey uses the international SI system of units.

teach.model: Use established terms, impersonal passive, and SI units. Examples: yapay zekâ, veri tabanı, donanım.

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
stages.hook: Can you use everything you have learned in one Turkish project?
explain: An integrated project combines reading, listening, speaking and writing. For example: research a Turkish topic (a city, a writer, a food), read two sources, listen to a short interview, give a three-minute presentation, and write a one-page report with an abstract. Evaluate yourself with CEFR-style descriptors (B2–C1): can you argue a position, summarise, and adjust register?

Checklist: accurate suffixes and harmony, consistent tense, clear connectors, correct register (sen/siz), and sources cited. Seek feedback from a native speaker and revise. Reflect: which structures still cause errors (cases, relative clauses, evidentiality)?

gq.q: Which skills does a project combine?
o: Only reading, in order to learn grammar
Only writing, in order to learn words
None of them; it is only for tests
gq.why: An integrated project combines reading, listening, speaking and writing in one task.
Feedback from a native speaker shows errors you cannot see yourself.

panel.why: Revising after feedback lets you correct errors and improve clarity.

o: Using only slang with every audience

panel.why: Choosing sen or siz to suit the audience shows control of register.

panel.q: What should a reflective learner do?
panel.why: Spotting recurring errors tells you what to practise next.

teach.model: Combine reading, listening, speaking and writing. Check suffixes, register and connectors. Get feedback and revise.
